item.title: Curvature's Impact on Hypersonic Boundary Layer Transition: A Numerical Study
item.description: This paper investigates how wall curvature influences the evolution of Mack modes in hypersonic boundary layers, a critical factor for boundary layer…
item.content:encoded:
Type: 💻 Numerical/CFD | Relevance: 75/100

This paper investigates how wall curvature influences the evolution of Mack modes in hypersonic boundary layers, a critical factor for boundary layer transition. The authors use linearized compressible Navier-Stokes equations to parametrically study flat-plate, concave, and convex curvatures, aiming to understand their impact on transition mechanisms. The work addresses a gap in understanding curvature effects on Mack modes in hypersonic flows, building upon existing research that primarily focuses on freestream parameters.

The study’s findings indicate that convex curvature stabilizes Mack modes due to favorable pressure gradients, while concave curvature destabilizes them through adverse pressure gradients. As curvature increases, these effects become more pronounced: greater convex curvature further suppresses Mack modes, and greater concave curvature amplifies them. The research provides a detailed numerical analysis of these physical phenomena.

Understanding these curvature effects is important for the design of hypersonic configurations, as boundary layer transition significantly affects aerodynamic heating and vehicle performance. The insights gained offer guidance for managing transition location, which is crucial for thermal management and overall vehicle integrity.

item.title: Quantifying Orion Aerodynamic Uncertainty with Structured Covariance Gaussian Networks
item.description: This paper introduces Structured Covariance Gaussian Networks (SCGNs), a new method for nonlinear regression and uncertainty quantification. The…
item.content:encoded:
Type: 🤖 ML/Aerodynamics | Relevance: 85/100

This paper introduces Structured Covariance Gaussian Networks (SCGNs), a new method for nonlinear regression and uncertainty quantification. The approach involves a pair of neural networks that parameterize the mean and a dense covariance function of a multivariate Gaussian process. These networks are trained together to maximize the log-likelihood of the observed data, with the covariance matrix constructed to ensure positive definiteness at every input. The authors also present a sampling technique to generate viable surrogate function realizations from the Gaussian process, applying the SCGN model to learn an aerodynamic response surface with built-in uncertainty for the Orion crew module.

The results indicate that SCGN provides an efficient and systematic way to learn complex nonlinear functional relationships and dense covariances. When compared to a baseline Gaussian process regressor, SCGN delivers comparable uncertainty descriptions while demonstrating improved scalability with increasing dataset size. The sample functions produced by SCGN are quick to evaluate online, making them suitable for integration into trajectory simulations.

These findings suggest that SCGN is a viable computational method for aerodynamic uncertainty quantification. Its ability to combine the flexibility of neural networks with the uncertainty quantification capabilities of Gaussian processes, particularly with improved scalability, holds promise for the design and analysis of high-speed vehicles where accurate aerodynamic predictions and their associated uncertainties are critical.
